moments.title: Brunelleschi's Baptistery experiment
moments.body:
Brunelleschi stages a perspective demonstration using a painted panel and a mirror in front of the Baptistery.

It is the first publicly documented demonstration of linear perspective.
moments.takeaway: An optical experiment, not a doctrine, set the path for Western visual representation.

moments.title: Alberti's De pictura
moments.body: Alberti's treatise codifies linear perspective as a teachable system. Italian into Latin translation makes it portable across Europe.
moments.takeaway: Codification transformed a workshop trick into a curriculum.

moments.title: Leonardo's Last Supper
moments.who: Leonardo da Vinci, Santa Maria delle Grazie
moments.body: Leonardo uses linear perspective converging on Christ's head to organise the composition's narrative.
moments.takeaway: Technical methods became carriers of theological and narrative meaning.

now.title: Perspective today
now.body: Linear perspective dominates photographic and digital imaging. Contemporary artists deliberately disrupt it (Hockney's polyptychs, computational rendering).
now.open_questions: How does machine vision, trained on perspective-rich images, encode (or fail to encode) other spatial conventions?

items.reflection: A single geometrical framework shaped how millions learned to read images and how cameras encode them.

moments.title: Salon des Refuses
moments.body: After widespread rejections from the official Salon, Napoleon III orders a parallel exhibition of refused works. Manet's Le Dejeuner sur l'herbe scandalises critics.
moments.takeaway: Even institutional efforts to manage controversy expanded what counted as exhibitable.

moments.title: First Impressionist exhibition
moments.who: Anonymous Society of Painters, Sculptors and Engravers
moments.body: Thirty artists, including Monet, Renoir, Degas and Pissarro, exhibit at Nadar's former studio. Critic Louis Leroy mocks Monet's Impression, soleil levant; the label sticks.
moments.takeaway: The name 'Impressionist' came from a hostile review, not the artists.

moments.title: Eighth and final group show
moments.body: Seurat exhibits A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, marking a turn towards post-impressionism. The group disbands.
moments.takeaway: Movements can dissolve precisely as their innovations become respectable.

now.title: Impressionism today
now.body: Once-radical works hang at the centre of national collections and attract enormous visitor numbers. Reception history is itself a field of study.
now.open_questions: What recent movements occupy the position Impressionism did at its 1874 launch?

items.reflection: Mass popular love for Impressionism makes it hard to remember how disruptive these paintings once were.

moments.title: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon
moments.body: Picasso completes Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, drawing on Iberian sculpture and African masks. The painting is shown to a small circle but not publicly exhibited until 1916.
moments.takeaway: Foundational works can circulate privately for years before public reception.

moments.title: Analytic and synthetic Cubism
moments.body: Working closely, the two artists develop fragmented, multi-viewpoint compositions, then introduce collage and synthetic Cubism with newspaper and oilcloth.
moments.takeaway: A movement was forged by two artists working in such close dialogue their canvases were sometimes hard to attribute.

moments.title: Guernica
moments.body: Picasso paints Guernica for the Spanish Pavilion at the Paris International Exposition, responding to the German bombing of the Basque town.
moments.takeaway: Modernist form became a vehicle for documentary political witness.

now.title: Cubism's legacy today
now.body: Cubist strategies appear across graphic design, animation and 3D modelling. Museum displays increasingly include Picasso's contemporary African and Iberian sources.
now.open_questions: How should museums display work that drew on cultural sources without credit?

items.reflection: What collaborators do together is harder to attribute than what a single artist makes alone.

moments.title: First readymade
moments.body: Duchamp mounts a bicycle wheel onto a stool in his studio. The combination is later cited as the first 'readymade'.
moments.takeaway: An informal studio experiment seeded a category that would outlast its physical examples.

moments.title: Fountain submitted
moments.body: A signed urinal is submitted to the Society of Independent Artists in New York. The committee refuses to display it. The original disappears; later versions are 1960s replicas.
moments.takeaway: The work's status as art became tied to the institutional refusal rather than the object itself.

moments.title: Fountain voted most influential 20th-century artwork
moments.body: A poll of 500 British art-world figures, organised by Gordon's gin in association with the Turner Prize, places Fountain first.
moments.takeaway: Cultural canonisation can crown the originally rejected.

now.title: Conceptual art today
now.body: Contemporary art frequently treats the idea as the work. Museum collections include certificates of authenticity for works that can be physically remade.
now.open_questions: How do generative AI and NFTs reframe the dematerialised art object?

items.reflection: Duchamp's gesture continues to organise debates about what counts as art, more than a century after the original urinal.

moments.title: Lascaux cave paintings
moments.body:
Hundreds of images of aurochs, horses and deer cover the limestone walls of Lascaux, painted by lamplight with mineral pigments and reed brushes.

The caves were discovered by four teenagers in September 1940.
moments.takeaway: Image-making is at least as old as agriculture, perhaps older.

moments.title: Chauvet earlier still
moments.body: Chauvet's lions, rhinoceroses and bears push the archaeological date of figurative painting back by tens of millennia.
moments.takeaway: What counts as the 'beginning' of art keeps moving as new caves are dated.

moments.title: Picasso visits Lascaux
moments.body: After visiting the newly discovered cave, Picasso reportedly remarked that modern artists had 'invented nothing'.
moments.takeaway: The deep past can rebuke claims of modern originality.

now.title: Prehistoric art today
now.body: Replica caves (Lascaux IV, 2016) protect the originals while opening them to visitors. Pigment analysis and 3D scanning continue to refine dating.
now.open_questions: What did these paintings mean to those who made them, and can we ever know?

items.reflection: Cave painting is the oldest continuous human visual tradition we know.

moments.title: Old Kingdom canon
moments.body: Egyptian art codifies proportional grids and the composite view (frontal eye, profile face, frontal torso) for over two millennia of remarkable consistency.
moments.takeaway: Style can persist for thousands of years when underpinned by ritual and instruction.

moments.title: Amarna naturalism
moments.body: Under Akhenaten, royal portraits adopt soft bellies, long faces and intimate family scenes, breaking with millennia of canon.
moments.takeaway: Even the longest-running styles can be disrupted by a single ruler's reforms.

moments.title: Tutankhamun's tomb opened
moments.who: Howard Carter, Valley of the Kings
moments.body: The discovery of an intact royal tomb floods European visual culture with Egyptian motifs, fuelling Art Deco.
moments.takeaway: Archaeological events ripple into contemporary design.

now.title: Egyptian collections today
now.body: Restitution debates surround the Rosetta Stone, the Nefertiti bust in Berlin and other works held in European museums.
now.open_questions: Where should objects from Egypt's ancient past be held and displayed?

items.reflection: Egyptian art lasted longer than the gap between Egypt and us.

moments.title: Parthenon sculptures
moments.body: Phidias supervises the Parthenon programme, including a colossal gold-and-ivory Athena and the now-dispersed frieze and metopes.
moments.takeaway: Classical Greek sculpture set proportions and poses Western art returned to for two millennia.

moments.title: Polykleitos's Doryphoros
moments.body: The Doryphoros embodies Polykleitos's written 'Canon' on proportion. Only Roman copies survive.
moments.takeaway: We know much classical sculpture only through later copies.

moments.title: Elgin removes the marbles
moments.body: Elgin removes around half the surviving Parthenon sculptures, later sold to the British Museum (1816).
moments.takeaway: The history of a work includes how it left its origin.

now.title: Restitution debates
now.body: Greece has campaigned for the return of the Parthenon marbles since the 1980s. Polychromy research shows ancient sculpture was vividly painted, not white.
now.open_questions: Should universal museums or origin states hold the world's most contested antiquities?

items.reflection: Our image of 'classical' is a 19th-century reconstruction as much as an ancient reality.

moments.title: San Vitale dedicated
moments.body: Mosaics of Justinian and Theodora face one another across the apse, set into shimmering gold ground.
moments.takeaway: Byzantine mosaics turned interior walls into spaces of imperial and divine display.

moments.title: Iconoclasm
moments.body: Two waves of iconoclasm destroy religious images across the empire. The Triumph of Orthodoxy in 843 restores icon veneration.
moments.takeaway: Image-destroying movements have repeatedly punctuated image-making traditions.

moments.title: Fall of Constantinople
moments.body: Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque; many icons are covered or destroyed; Greek scholars flee west, fuelling the Renaissance.
moments.takeaway: Political collapse moves artistic knowledge across borders.

now.title: Byzantine art today
now.body: Hagia Sophia returned to mosque use in 2020. Orthodox icon traditions remain vibrant in Greece, Russia and the diaspora.
now.open_questions: How should sites with successive religious uses be presented to visitors?

items.reflection: Byzantine art treated images as direct windows to the divine, not as representations.

moments.title: Saint-Denis choir dedicated
moments.body: Suger rebuilds the choir of Saint-Denis using pointed arches, ribbed vaults and large stained-glass windows, articulating an aesthetics of light.
moments.takeaway: Gothic architecture had a documented theological programme.

moments.title: Notre-Dame de Paris
moments.body: Construction of Notre-Dame spans nearly two centuries. The flying buttress enables thinner walls and vast windows.
moments.takeaway: Cathedrals were generational projects whose designers rarely saw completion.

moments.title: Notre-Dame fire
moments.body: The cathedral's spire and roof collapse on 15 April 2019. A reopening follows on 7 December 2024.
moments.takeaway: Major monuments live through cycles of damage and restoration.

now.title: Gothic now
now.body: Gothic revival shaped 19th-century parliament buildings and universities. Conservation debates after fires (Notre-Dame, Glasgow School of Art) shape how we treat lost work.
now.open_questions: Should restorations recreate the lost or visibly mark the new?

items.reflection: A century after they were sneered at as 'Gothic' (i.e. barbaric), these cathedrals became Europe's defining monuments.

moments.title: Dome competition
moments.who: Filippo Brunelleschi and Lorenzo Ghiberti, Florence
moments.body: Florence Cathedral's wardens hold a competition for completing the cathedral's open crossing. Brunelleschi wins with a self-supporting double-shell design.
moments.takeaway: The Renaissance's signature dome was a problem-solving project, not just an artistic vision.

moments.title: Dome completed
moments.body: The 45-metre cupola of Santa Maria del Fiore is consecrated. Brunelleschi invents hoisting machinery to lift over 4 million bricks.
moments.takeaway: Major architecture often advances tooling as much as design.

moments.title: Brunelleschi dies
moments.body: He is buried inside the cathedral. The dome remains the largest masonry dome in the world.
moments.takeaway: Some innovations have never been technically equalled.

now.title: Renaissance engineering today
now.body: Structural engineers still study the dome's herringbone brickwork. Florence's silhouette remains shaped by Brunelleschi's solution.
now.open_questions: How should we tell stories of art and engineering together rather than as separate disciplines?

items.reflection: Renaissance 'art' included the technical mastery to build at scale.

moments.title: Holy Trinity fresco
moments.body: The fresco employs Brunelleschi's perspective for the first time at architectural scale. Viewers stand on the church floor as if before a real chapel.
moments.takeaway: Perspective went from drawing-board experiment to monumental painting in under a decade.

moments.title: Masaccio dies
moments.body: Masaccio dies aged 26, having completed only a handful of works including the Brancacci Chapel scenes.
moments.takeaway: Foundational figures sometimes leave thin bodies of work.

moments.title: Brancacci restored
moments.body: Cleaning reveals colours obscured by candle soot and earlier varnish, allowing closer study of Masaccio's technique alongside Masolino and Filippino Lippi.
moments.takeaway: Conservation can rewrite art history.

now.title: Early Renaissance now
now.body: Florence remains a teaching ground for Western art history students. The Brancacci Chapel is undergoing further investigation through the 2020s.
now.open_questions: How do digital reconstructions change what we can see and what we lose?

items.reflection: A young painter, dead at 26, set the agenda for the next 500 years of Western painting.

moments.title: Mona Lisa
moments.body: Leonardo carries the panel with him for years, working on the soft modelling (sfumato) of face and landscape. He never delivers it to the patron.
moments.takeaway: Some of art history's most famous works were never finished in the patron's sense.

moments.title: Vitruvian Man
moments.body: The drawing combines anatomical observation with Vitruvius's proportions, an emblem of Renaissance synthesis.
moments.takeaway: Leonardo's notebooks blur the line between art and natural philosophy.

moments.title: Mona Lisa stolen
moments.body: An Italian workman takes the painting from its frame and keeps it for two years. The theft makes it world-famous.
moments.takeaway: Fame can be made by crime as well as quality.

now.title: Leonardo today
now.body: Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million in 2017 amid disputes over attribution. Anatomical drawings continue to be studied for their accuracy.
now.open_questions: How should attribution debates be communicated to museum visitors?

items.reflection: Leonardo left fewer than 20 paintings but a thousand drawings; the drawings show how he thought.

moments.title: Sistine Chapel ceiling
moments.body: Michelangelo paints over 300 figures across 500 square metres of vault, working largely standing rather than lying down.
moments.takeaway: The Sistine ceiling was painted at speed under intense papal pressure.

moments.title: Last Judgement
moments.body: The fresco's nudes are partially overpainted with 'breeches' after Michelangelo's death.
moments.takeaway: Even masterpieces are edited by later centuries.

moments.title: Sistine cleaning
moments.body: Cleaning reveals far brighter colours than expected, prompting debate about whether some shading had been removed.
moments.takeaway: Conservation choices are art-historical arguments.

now.title: Michelangelo now
now.body: The Sistine Chapel receives roughly five million visitors a year. Climate and crowd control are ongoing conservation challenges.
now.open_questions: How can major sites balance access with preservation?

items.reflection: Michelangelo wrote in a letter, 'I am no painter'. The ceiling argues otherwise.

moments.title: Durer's Christ-like self-portrait
moments.body: Durer paints himself frontally in the pose conventionally reserved for Christ, signed and dated in Latin.
moments.takeaway: The artist as creator becomes an explicit theme in early modern self-portraiture.

moments.title: Apocalypse woodcuts
moments.body: Durer publishes his Apocalypse series, exploiting print to distribute large-format images at unprecedented scale.
moments.takeaway: Print transformed both religious image culture and an artist's reach.

moments.title: Treatise on measurement
moments.body: Durer publishes the first geometry book in German for a non-specialist audience, applying mathematics to drawing.
moments.takeaway: Northern Renaissance artists were also teachers of theory.

now.title: Print after Durer
now.body: Engraving and woodcut remain studied techniques. Durer's monogram is among the earliest persistent artist brands.
now.open_questions: What is the print equivalent in the age of AI image generation?

items.reflection: Print made an artist's image distributable centuries before mass photography.

moments.title: Saint Matthew cycle
moments.body: Caravaggio's three canvases use a single dramatic shaft of light to organise narrative across a chapel.
moments.takeaway: Baroque painting often treated light itself as the principal actor.

moments.title: Caravaggio flees Rome
moments.body: After killing a man in a duel, he flees to Naples, Malta and Sicily, painting major altarpieces under the pressure of exile.
moments.takeaway: Some of art history's most influential late work was made on the run.

moments.title: Death on the beach
moments.body: Caravaggio dies aged 38, possibly of fever, while trying to return to Rome under expected pardon.
moments.takeaway: His career lasted only about 15 active years.

now.title: Caravaggio rediscovered
now.body: After centuries of disregard, Caravaggio's reputation was rebuilt in the 20th century, especially by Roberto Longhi.
now.open_questions: How do we balance an artist's biography with the works themselves?

items.reflection: Caravaggio's lighting is now the visual grammar of half of cinema.

moments.title: Trial in Rome
moments.body: Aged 17, Gentileschi gives evidence under torture (thumbscrews) in the trial of her painter-tutor Agostino Tassi for rape.
moments.takeaway: Art history's documentary record sometimes preserves traumatic testimony alongside artistic biography.

moments.title: Judith Slaying Holofernes
moments.body: Her painting of Judith and her maidservant beheading Holofernes is unusually muscular and unsentimental.
moments.takeaway: Subject matter and biography can be read in close dialogue.

moments.title: London
moments.body: Gentileschi joins her father Orazio at Charles I's court, working on ceiling decorations for the Queen's House at Greenwich.
moments.takeaway: Major women painters worked internationally despite later neglect by canon-makers.

now.title: Recovering women artists
now.body: Major exhibitions (London 2020, Paris 2024) have placed Gentileschi at the centre of Baroque studies. Linda Nochlin's 1971 essay 'Why have there been no great women artists?' frames the rediscovery.
now.open_questions: How do museums tell the histories of artists whose work was attributed to men?

items.reflection: Restoring Gentileschi to the canon is also restoring a piece of court politics, law and image-making.

moments.title: Apollo and Daphne
moments.body: Bernini sculpts Daphne mid-transformation into a laurel tree, with fingertips becoming leaves and bark climbing her body.
moments.takeaway: Bernini made marble appear to move.

moments.title: Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
moments.body: Bernini stages the saint's mystical vision in a marble theatre, with concealed lighting from above.
moments.takeaway: Baroque sculpture often used architecture and light as collaborators.

moments.title: Saint Peter's Square colonnade
moments.body: Bernini's two arcs of columns 'embrace' pilgrims arriving at the Vatican.
moments.takeaway: Urban-scale sculpture choreographs the visitor's body and gaze.

now.title: Bernini's Rome today
now.body: Most of Bernini's works remain at their original sites. Conservation in Roman pollution is an ongoing concern.
now.open_questions: How should religious sculpture be presented to increasingly secular audiences?

items.reflection: Bernini was an architect, sculptor, painter and theatre designer at once.

moments.title: Las Meninas
moments.body: Velazquez paints himself before a vast canvas, the Infanta Margarita, courtiers and the king and queen reflected in a back mirror.
moments.takeaway: A 17th-century painting becomes a meditation on representation itself.

moments.title: Velazquez dies
moments.body: Velazquez dies after decorating quarters for the Pyrenees marriage of Maria Theresa to Louis XIV.
moments.takeaway: Court painters' careers were closely tied to royal politics.

moments.title: Picasso's 58 Meninas variations
moments.body: Picasso paints 58 variations on Las Meninas in five months, now housed at the Museu Picasso in Barcelona.
moments.takeaway: Major works keep generating dialogue with later artists.

now.title: Velazquez today
now.body: Las Meninas remains the Prado's central painting. Foucault opens 'The Order of Things' (1966) with a long reading of it.
now.open_questions: What kinds of representation are still impossible to depict?

items.reflection: A single court group portrait keeps philosophers, painters and audiences arguing four centuries later.

moments.title: A Harlot's Progress
moments.body: Hogarth pioneers the 'modern moral subject', a series of paintings turned into prints for the urban middle class.
moments.takeaway: Eighteenth-century print culture created new audiences for serial narrative art.

moments.title: Engraving Copyright Act
moments.body: Lobbied by Hogarth, the act protects engravers from piracy and is sometimes called 'Hogarth's Act'.
moments.takeaway: Artists shaped copyright law to protect their print income.

moments.title: Royal Academy founded
moments.body: Joshua Reynolds is its first president; annual Summer Exhibitions begin in 1769.
moments.takeaway: National institutions defined what 'serious' British art could look like.

now.title: British art institutions today
now.body: Tate, the Royal Academy and regional collections share the conversation. Hogarth's series are again studied as graphic-novel precursors.
now.open_questions: Who are the inheritors of Hogarth's serial visual storytelling in the digital age?

items.reflection: Hogarth wanted to be remembered as a moralist; he also invented print marketing for paintings.

moments.title: Los Caprichos published
moments.body: Goya's 80 etchings satirise Spanish church, court and superstition. He withdraws them under pressure from the Inquisition.
moments.takeaway: Print became a vehicle for politically risky satire under censorship.

moments.title: Third of May 1808
moments.body: Goya paints the execution of Madrid civilians by Napoleonic troops, a scene of modern atrocity without classical heroism.
moments.takeaway: Modern history painting could depict victims rather than victors.

moments.title: Black Paintings
moments.body: Goya covers the walls of his house with 14 nightmarish oils, including 'Saturn Devouring His Son'. They are transferred to canvas in the 1870s.
moments.takeaway: Some of art history's most personal works were never intended for public view.

now.title: Goya now
now.body: The Disasters of War prints (made 1810-1820, published 1863) remain a baseline for war art. Goya's paintings are central to the Prado.
now.open_questions: How does an artist's late, private work get integrated into the canon?

items.reflection: Goya saw the end of the old world and the beginning of modern violence, and painted both.

moments.title: The Fighting Temeraire
moments.body: Turner paints the warship Temeraire being towed by a steam tug to be broken up, a transitional image between sail and steam.
moments.takeaway: Turner painted technology change as elegiac, not merely heroic.

moments.title: Snow Storm
moments.body: Turner claims to have had himself tied to the mast of a steamboat in a storm to paint the scene. The story is contested but characteristic.
moments.takeaway: Romantic painters narrated their own pursuit of extreme experience.

moments.title: Turner dies
moments.body: Turner leaves nearly 300 oil paintings and 30,000 works on paper to the nation. Most are now at Tate Britain.
moments.takeaway: An artist's bequest can shape national collections.

now.title: Turner today
now.body: The Turner Prize, founded in 1984, continues his name. Climate-science illustration sometimes uses his weather paintings as visual references.
now.open_questions: Can a 19th-century painter help us see today's atmospheric change?

items.reflection: Turner painted weather as a subject in itself, decades before Impressionism.

moments.title: The Hay Wain
moments.body: Constable paints a rural scene of his Suffolk childhood with carefully observed cloud studies.
moments.takeaway: Constable made the English countryside a serious subject for ambitious painting.

moments.title: Paris Salon gold medal
moments.body: The Hay Wain wins a gold medal at the Paris Salon, influencing Delacroix and the Barbizon school.
moments.takeaway: British painting fed continental Romanticism.

moments.title: Constable dies
moments.body: Constable's work becomes a national icon, reproduced on biscuit tins, posters and stamps.
moments.takeaway: Mass reproduction can both popularise and dilute a painter's reputation.

now.title: Landscape and ecology
now.body: 21st-century landscape art often engages climate, agriculture and access to land.
now.open_questions: What is the contemporary equivalent of Constable's village pond?

items.reflection: Constable saw a particular valley and made it everyone's idea of rural England.

moments.title: Liberty Leading the People
moments.body: Painted in response to the July Revolution, the canvas places an allegorical Liberty among the dead and the living of the barricades.
moments.takeaway: Romanticism could be both classical and journalistic.

moments.title: Voyage to Morocco
moments.body: His sketchbooks from North Africa fuel decades of 'Orientalist' painting.
moments.takeaway: European travel reshaped, and distorted, depictions of the rest of the world.

moments.title: Liberty in the Mediatheque
moments.body: Cleaning reveals Delacroix's palette more clearly; the painting remains a Louvre touchstone.
moments.takeaway: Conservation continues to update our view of canonical works.

now.title: Romanticism's legacy
now.body: Delacroix's image is still reused on banknotes, posters and protest art across the political spectrum.
now.open_questions: Who owns the image of 'liberty'?

items.reflection: A painting made in 1830 still appears at almost every modern protest.

moments.title: The Stone Breakers
moments.body: Courbet paints two ordinary labourers at life size in a scene previously reserved for myth or history.
moments.takeaway: Realism elevated ordinary workers to the scale of history painting.

moments.title: Pavilion of Realism
moments.body: Rejected from the Exposition Universelle, Courbet builds his own pavilion to show his work alongside a 'manifesto of realism'.
moments.takeaway: Artists began to organise their own exhibitions outside official channels.

moments.title: The Gleaners
moments.body: Millet's painting of three peasant women gathering leftover grain becomes a touchstone of social realism.
moments.takeaway: Rural labour was a recurring concern of mid-19th-century European painting.

now.title: Realism today
now.body: Documentary photography and politically engaged painting still trace lineage to Courbet and Millet.
now.open_questions: Who counts as a 'worker' in 21st-century image-making?

items.reflection: Realism is itself a stylistic choice, not a neutral mirror.

moments.title: Le Dejeuner sur l'herbe
moments.body: Manet paints a clothed picnic with a nude woman who stares directly at the viewer, scandalising Paris.
moments.takeaway: Eye contact and contemporary clothing made nudity look new.

moments.title: Olympia exhibited
moments.body: Olympia, a courtesan with a black servant, receives such a hostile reception that guards have to be posted.
moments.takeaway: Modernism began at the intersection of class, race and gender provocation.

moments.title: Laure restored to history
moments.body: An exhibition 'Le modele noir' centres Olympia's servant Laure, restoring black sitters to French art history.
moments.takeaway: Canonical images keep yielding new readings.

now.title: Manet now
now.body: Manet sits at the hinge between Realism and Impressionism. Major exhibitions continue (Musee d'Orsay 2023).
now.open_questions: Whose look organises a painting, and who gets named?

items.reflection: Manet's scandals helped define what counted as modern.

moments.title: Impression, soleil levant
moments.body: Monet paints the harbour at dawn in 30 minutes. The painting names the entire movement.
moments.takeaway: A casual title can define a movement against the painter's wishes.

moments.title: Series painting
moments.body: Monet paints haystacks, the cathedral facade and the Houses of Parliament under shifting light, producing dozens of canvases per motif.
moments.takeaway: Series painting treated time and atmosphere as the subject.

moments.title: Water Lilies
moments.body: Half-blind from cataracts, Monet paints monumental water lily panels for the Musee de l'Orangerie. The donation is finalised in 1927.
moments.takeaway: Late style can be both physically constrained and ambitious.

now.title: Monet's blockbuster afterlife
now.body: Immersive Monet exhibitions sell out worldwide. His Giverny garden is preserved and replanted as a working studio environment.
now.open_questions: What is left to see in a painter shown this much?

items.reflection: Painting the same motif many times is both a study in light and a study in the painter.

moments.title: Eight Impressionist shows
moments.body: Pissarro is the only artist to exhibit in all eight Impressionist exhibitions; Degas, Renoir, Monet, Cezanne and others contribute selectively.
moments.takeaway: A 'movement' was held together by particular relationships and quarrels.

moments.title: Degas's dancers
moments.body: Degas paints and pastels the Paris Opera ballet, often from above and behind the scenes.
moments.takeaway: Impressionism included indoor urban subjects, not just gardens.

moments.title: Little Dancer Aged Fourteen
moments.body: Degas exhibits a wax figure dressed in real tulle and silk. The mixed-media sculpture is unprecedented.
moments.takeaway: Impressionist sculpture and painting often experimented with materials.

now.title: Impressionist circle today
now.body: Curators increasingly highlight Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt's roles alongside the male core. Pissarro's Jewish-Caribbean background is studied as part of the story.
now.open_questions: Who is missing from familiar narratives of canonical movements?

items.reflection: Impressionism was a network as much as a style.

moments.title: Mont Sainte-Victoire series
moments.body: Cezanne paints the same mountain dozens of times, building form from patches of colour rather than line.
moments.takeaway: Cezanne moved from Impressionist sensation toward analytical structure.

moments.title: First major Cezanne show
moments.body: Vollard organises a one-man exhibition that establishes Cezanne's reputation among younger painters.
moments.takeaway: Dealers shaped which late 19th-century artists became canonical.

moments.title: Cezanne retrospective
moments.body: Posthumous retrospective inspires both Matisse and Picasso. Picasso later calls Cezanne 'the father of us all'.
moments.takeaway: One painter's solution to landscape became another's path to abstraction.

now.title: Cezanne now
now.body: Tate Modern's 2022 Cezanne retrospective drew large audiences. His correspondence is published as a key source.
now.open_questions: How do we teach a painter who is the bridge between two eras?

items.reflection: Cezanne worked alone for years; the next generation worked from him.

moments.title: Arles
moments.body: Van Gogh moves to Arles and paints sunflowers, bedroom interiors and night cafes in less than two years.
moments.takeaway: Bursts of intense productivity can compress a career.

moments.title: Gauguin arrives
moments.who: Paul Gauguin and Van Gogh, Arles
moments.body: Two months of joint work end in argument and Van Gogh's self-mutilation of his ear.
moments.takeaway: Artistic collaborations carry biographical risk.

moments.title: Death at Auvers
moments.body: Van Gogh dies at 37 after a gunshot wound. His brother Theo dies six months later. Theo's widow Jo van Gogh-Bonger spends decades promoting his work.
moments.takeaway: Posthumous recognition often depends on family stewardship.

now.title: Van Gogh's afterlife
now.body: His paintings are among the most reproduced in the world. The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam (1973) holds the largest collection.
now.open_questions: How should the artist's mental illness be discussed alongside the work?

items.reflection: Van Gogh sold one painting in life; the world hasn't stopped buying them since.

moments.title: Sunday on La Grande Jatte
moments.body: Seurat paints over two years using small dots of pure colour mixed in the viewer's eye, drawing on Chevreul's colour theory.
moments.takeaway: Late 19th-century painting was in dialogue with optical science.

moments.title: Last Impressionist show
moments.body: La Grande Jatte is exhibited at the eighth Impressionist exhibition. The label 'neo-impressionism' is coined.
moments.takeaway: New movements branched off public exhibitions.

moments.title: Seurat dies
moments.body: Seurat dies aged 31 of probable meningitis, leaving a small but influential body of work.
moments.takeaway: Short careers can still redirect a tradition.

now.title: Pointillism now
now.body: Pixels and halftone dots in modern reproduction echo Seurat's logic. Sondheim's musical Sunday in the Park with George (1984) brought the painting to a new audience.
now.open_questions: What other 19th-century optical experiments anticipated digital images?

items.reflection: A painter who explained colour theory could not stop colour from changing on him.

moments.title: Salon d'Automne
moments.who: Henri Matisse, Andre Derain, Maurice de Vlaminck
moments.body: Critic Louis Vauxcelles calls them 'fauves' ('wild beasts'); the label sticks.
moments.takeaway: Like Impressionism, Fauvism was named by a hostile critic.

moments.title: Notes of a Painter
moments.body: Matisse publishes his theoretical essay on expression through colour and composition rather than imitation.
moments.takeaway: Modernist painters wrote their own theory.

moments.title: Cut-outs
moments.body: Bed-ridden after surgery, Matisse cuts painted paper into large-scale compositions ('The Snail', 'Blue Nudes').
moments.takeaway: Late style turned physical limitation into formal liberation.

now.title: Matisse now
now.body: Tate Modern's 2014 cut-out show was its most visited exhibition. Matisse remains central to colour pedagogy.
now.open_questions: What kinds of disability narratives belong in art history?

items.reflection: Matisse cut paper as gladly as some painters use a brush.

moments.title: Futurist Manifesto
moments.body: Marinetti publishes the manifesto on the front page of Le Figaro, glorifying speed, machines and war.
moments.takeaway: Avant-garde movements increasingly arrived as manifestos before paintings.

moments.title: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space
moments.body: Boccioni's bronze striding figure captures motion as a sculptural surface.
moments.takeaway: Futurism translated dynamism from physics into form.

moments.title: Boccioni dies
moments.body: Boccioni dies in a military riding accident at 33. Futurism continues but loses momentum.
moments.takeaway: Movements depend on individual lives.

now.title: Futurism reconsidered
now.body: Futurism's later entanglement with Italian Fascism is now central to its critical discussion.
now.open_questions: How should we display art whose politics we reject?

items.reflection: Avant-gardes are not always politically progressive.

moments.title: Die Brucke founded
moments.who: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and friends, Dresden
moments.body: A group of architecture students forms an artists' collective drawing on woodcut, non-Western art and urban life.
moments.takeaway: German Expressionism began as an architecture-student commune.

moments.title: Der Blaue Reiter
moments.body: Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc form a parallel group with a more spiritual programme.
moments.takeaway: Expressionism was a constellation, not a single school.

moments.title: Degenerate Art exhibition
moments.body: The regime mounts an exhibition mocking modernist work; many Expressionist paintings are confiscated or destroyed.
moments.takeaway: Modernism was a target of state violence.

now.title: Expressionism today
now.body: Restitution claims continue for works looted from Jewish collectors. Kirchner's Berlin street scenes are central to German modernism collections.
now.open_questions: How should restitution be balanced with public display?

items.reflection: Expressionism's politics changed less than its enemies did.

moments.title: Cabaret Voltaire
moments.body: Refugees in neutral Switzerland stage performances of nonsense poetry, masks and noise, calling it Dada.
moments.takeaway: Dada was a wartime response to the failure of reason.

moments.title: Berlin Dada Fair
moments.who: Hannah Hoch, John Heartfield, George Grosz
moments.body: Photomontage emerges as a Dada technique with clear political bite.
moments.takeaway: Cut-and-paste image-making has political roots.

moments.title: Surrealist Manifesto
moments.body: Breton's manifesto announces Surrealism, building on Dada and psychoanalysis.
moments.takeaway: Avant-gardes morph into one another.

now.title: Dada now
now.body: Photomontage techniques recur in protest and meme culture. The MoMA centennial show (2024-25) returned Dada to wide attention.
now.open_questions: Is meme culture today's Dada?

items.reflection: Dada's anti-art is now firmly inside the art museum.

moments.title: Black Square
moments.body: Malevich exhibits 'Black Square' hung in the upper corner of the gallery, the position traditionally reserved for icons in Russian homes.
moments.takeaway: Suprematism positioned abstract painting at the spiritual level of icons.

moments.title: Russian Revolution
moments.body: Avant-garde artists initially align with the new state. Malevich teaches at Vitebsk and elsewhere.
moments.takeaway: Abstraction briefly looked like the art of revolution.

moments.title: Malevich's funeral
moments.body: Malevich is buried in a Suprematist-decorated coffin, his last public statement under increasingly hostile Stalinist cultural policy.
moments.takeaway: Avant-gardes were destroyed by the politics that briefly hosted them.

now.title: Suprematism today
now.body: Black Square is central to Russian modernism collections. X-rays reveal an earlier composition beneath the surface.
now.open_questions: How should provocative under-drawings be communicated to audiences?

items.reflection: An abstract painting can carry as much history as a portrait.

moments.title: De Stijl founded
moments.who: Theo van Doesburg, Piet Mondrian, Leiden
moments.body: The journal De Stijl publishes its first issue, calling for a 'new plastic art' of straight lines and primary colours.
moments.takeaway: Dutch modernism arrived through a journal as much as paintings.

moments.title: Schroder House
moments.body: Rietveld designs a house with sliding walls and primary-colour furnishings, a built version of De Stijl theory.
moments.takeaway: Modernist painting was inseparable from architecture and furniture.

moments.title: Broadway Boogie Woogie
moments.body: In exile, Mondrian translates Manhattan's grid and jazz into a final yellow-blue composition.
moments.takeaway: Exile reshaped European modernism in American cities.

now.title: De Stijl now
now.body: Mondrian's compositions appear on Yves Saint Laurent dresses (1965) and countless products. Authorised reproductions debate where art ends and product design begins.
now.open_questions: Can a grid be a brand?

items.reflection: Painting that wanted to dissolve into design did so, eventually.

moments.title: Early Sunday Morning
moments.body: Hopper paints a Manhattan street empty of people, with sharp shadows from a low sun.
moments.takeaway: American Scene painting put silence at the centre.

moments.title: Nighthawks
moments.body: Hopper paints four figures in a diner at night, weeks after Pearl Harbor.
moments.takeaway: Wartime images of solitude have lasted as American icons.

moments.title: Edward Hopper goes viral
moments.body: His paintings circulate on social media as images of pandemic isolation.
moments.takeaway: Twentieth-century paintings can find new audiences in a crisis.

now.title: Hopper now
now.body: The Whitney holds the largest Hopper collection. His scenes underpin photography, cinema and graphic novels.
now.open_questions: What images will mark the present as Nighthawks marks 1942?

items.reflection: Hopper painted Americans not talking to each other long before phones.

moments.title: Pollock's drip technique
moments.body: Pollock lays canvas on the floor and drips industrial enamel from sticks and brushes, working from all four sides.
moments.takeaway: Process became the subject of the painting.

moments.title: Life magazine profile
moments.body: Life magazine asks 'Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?' Mass media turn an avant-garde painter into a national figure.
moments.takeaway: Magazines built post-war American art's audience.

moments.title: Rothko Chapel commission
moments.body: Rothko begins paintings for an ecumenical chapel, completed posthumously in 1971.
moments.takeaway: Abstract Expressionism reached for religious scale.

now.title: Abstract Expressionism now
now.body: Lee Krasner, Joan Mitchell and Helen Frankenthaler are now recognised as central, not adjacent.
now.open_questions: How should we narrate movements that were sold as men-only?

items.reflection: Drip paintings look spontaneous and were not.

moments.title: Just what is it that makes today's homes...?
moments.body: Hamilton's collage for the 'This Is Tomorrow' exhibition prefigures Pop's love of advertising and consumer imagery.
moments.takeaway: British Pop predates American Pop.

moments.title: Campbell's Soup Cans
moments.body: Warhol exhibits 32 canvases, one for each soup variety. The Ferus Gallery sells most for around $100 each.
moments.takeaway: Mass-production imagery became gallery painting.

moments.title: Whaam!
moments.body: Lichtenstein paints a fighter plane attack in Ben-Day dots, magnifying comic-book style.
moments.takeaway: Pop turned popular print into high art.

now.title: Pop today
now.body: Warhol's Marilyn diptych and other works regularly set auction records. Brand image debates persist around Hockney, Koons and KAWS.
now.open_questions: What is the line between Pop and product?

items.reflection: Pop made the question 'is this art?' part of the work itself.

moments.title: Specific Objects essay
moments.body: Judd argues for an art that is neither painting nor sculpture but a third category: the 'specific object'.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical essays helped artists carve out new categories.

moments.title: Marfa, Texas
moments.body: Judd installs permanent works on a former army base, controlling their context.
moments.takeaway: Some artists rebelled against the gallery as a unit.

moments.title: Art After Philosophy
moments.body: Kosuth argues art's value lies in the idea, building Conceptual art's theoretical base.
moments.takeaway: Minimal and Conceptual art shared a stripping back of the visual.

now.title: Minimalism now
now.body: Marfa is a pilgrimage site. Minimalism inspires contemporary architecture and product design.
now.open_questions: What does 'less' mean in a high-resolution age?

items.reflection: Minimalism made looking slowly into a practice.

moments.title: Daguerreotype announced
moments.body: The French Academy of Sciences publishes Daguerre's process. France purchases the rights and gives them to the world.
moments.takeaway: Photography began as a state-sponsored gift.

moments.title: Decisive moment
moments.body: Cartier-Bresson articulates a philosophy of photography as the capture of fleeting visual order. His book 'Images a la sauvette' appears in 1952.
moments.takeaway: Photography developed its own aesthetic vocabulary.

moments.title: Untitled Film Stills
moments.body: Sherman photographs herself as imaginary actresses in 1950s-60s films, beginning a long inquiry into the constructed self.
moments.takeaway: Photography became a tool for theorising identity, not just recording it.

now.title: Photography now
now.body: Phone cameras outproduce all earlier photography combined. AI image generation reframes what 'taking a picture' means.
now.open_questions: What counts as photography when the image is synthesised?

items.reflection: Photography has been declared 'finished' at every technological turn and never has been.

moments.title: Freeze exhibition
moments.body: Hirst curates 'Freeze' in a disused warehouse with fellow Goldsmiths students. It launches the YBA generation.
moments.takeaway: Student-organised shows can launch national movements.

moments.title: The Physical Impossibility of Death
moments.body: Hirst suspends a 4-metre tiger shark in formaldehyde. Charles Saatchi commissions it for around 50,000 pounds.
moments.takeaway: YBA work was inseparable from collector patronage.

moments.title: Banksy shreds
moments.body: 'Girl with Balloon' partially self-shreds during a Sotheby's auction. It is renamed 'Love is in the Bin'.
moments.takeaway: Contemporary art keeps merging with its own auction theatre.

now.title: Britain's contemporary scene
now.body: London's commercial galleries face Brexit and Asian competition. Banksy's identity remains contested; his works increasingly attract restoration arguments.
now.open_questions: Should street art be preserved at all?

items.reflection: Late 20th-century British art was as much about market as making.

moments.title: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji
moments.body: Hokusai's series, including 'The Great Wave', is printed in tens of thousands of impressions across many runs.
moments.takeaway: Edo-period print was already mass image culture.

moments.title: Japan opens to trade
moments.body: American gunboat diplomacy ends Japan's seclusion. Japanese prints flow to Europe as wrapping paper and trade goods.
moments.takeaway: Diplomacy and packaging carried art history.

moments.title: Japonisme in Paris
moments.body: European artists collect and copy ukiyo-e, transforming compositional approaches.
moments.takeaway: Impressionism's flat colour and high horizons drew on Japanese print.

now.title: Ukiyo-e now
now.body: The Great Wave is among the most reproduced images in the world. The British Museum holds a major collection.
now.open_questions: How can we untangle 'influence' from appropriation?

items.reflection: What looked Parisian and modern often had a Japanese woodblock behind it.

moments.title: Robie House
moments.body: Wright completes a defining Prairie-style house with long horizontals and integrated interiors.
moments.takeaway: American modern architecture had its own roots.

moments.title: Fallingwater
moments.body: Wright designs the Kaufmann family house cantilevered over a waterfall.
moments.takeaway: Modern architecture could be deeply rooted in landscape.

moments.title: Guggenheim opens
moments.body: Wright dies six months before the museum opens with its single sloped ramp.
moments.takeaway: Some architects die before their major buildings host visitors.

now.title: Wright's legacy
now.body: Eight of Wright's buildings are now UNESCO World Heritage. Conservation challenges include leaking roofs and dated structural systems.
now.open_questions: How do we preserve modern materials never meant to last centuries?

items.reflection: An American architect rejected European modernism and built his own.

moments.title: Peak competition win
moments.body: Hadid wins The Peak competition with sharp, fragmented drawings inspired by Suprematism. The project is unbuilt.
moments.takeaway: Unbuilt projects can define a reputation.

moments.title: Pritzker Prize
moments.body: Hadid becomes the first woman to win architecture's top prize.
moments.takeaway: Architecture's most visible awards were almost exclusively male until 2004.

moments.title: Hadid dies
moments.body: Hadid dies at 65; her firm continues completing major works (Beijing's Daxing Airport, 2019).
moments.takeaway: Posthumous practice raises authorship questions.

now.title: Contemporary architecture
now.body: Parametric design tools democratise complex geometry. Critics ask whether iconic buildings have outlived their cultural use.
now.open_questions: Who designs the buildings of the global south?

items.reflection: A Baghdad-born architect in London changed what curves were possible.

moments.title: Infinity Mirror Room
moments.body: Kusama exhibits 'Infinity Mirror Room - Phalli's Field', filling a room with stuffed soft sculptures and mirrors.
moments.takeaway: Immersive installation has roots in the 1960s.

moments.title: Return to Japan
moments.body: Kusama returns to Japan and voluntarily enters a psychiatric hospital where she still lives and works.
moments.takeaway: Some artists organise their lives around continuous studio practice.

moments.title: Mass audience
moments.body: Touring Infinity Room exhibitions sell out worldwide and become signature 'Instagrammable' shows.
moments.takeaway: Social media reshaped which contemporary art reaches mass audiences.

now.title: Kusama now
now.body: Kusama is among the world's bestselling living artists. Louis Vuitton collaborations spread her dots globally.
now.open_questions: What happens to art designed around photography?

items.reflection: Kusama has been making the same world for 70 years; the world finally walked in.
